To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the IC2 on chromosome 7 is a long-range silencer of paternally imprinted genes in the placenta and is able to silence genes independently of DNA methyation.

the paternally repressive chromatin at the distal chromosome 2 imprinting center is maintained independently of DNA methylation and is required for the imprinting of several genes in trophoblast cells.
histone methylation maintains imprinting in the placenta independently of DNA methylation.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the molecular mechanisms underlying genomic imprinting.
the epigenetic regulation of gene expression in the mammalian placenta, and how this is controlled by the imprinting center.
the molecular mechanisms underlying the regulation of gene expression during development.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the paternal chromosome is marked by repressive histones in the trophblast independently of DNA methyaltion and that the IC2 is responsible for this.
DNA methylation is not required to maintain the imprinting of the genes in the cluster in trophoblast cells.
DNA methylation is not required for imprinting of the genes in the placenta.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the IC2 region of distal chromosome 6 in mice contains at least 4 genes, including the Igf2 and H19 genes that are paternally expressed in the embryonic tissues, and the Cdkn1c and Slc38a4 genes that are patenally expressed in the placenta only.

the imprinting center (IC) 2 on distal chromosome-7 of mouse is required for the establishment and maintenance of imprinted expression in the placenta of the paternally repressive domain, which contains the paternally expressed genes Peg3 and Peg11, and the maternally expressed genes Dlk1 and Gtl2.

IC2 is a cis-acting imprinting center that is required for the recruitment of a repressive chromatin mark (H3K9me3) that is essential for the silencing of a large imprinted cluster of genes in the trophobastr (placenta), independently of DNA methylations.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the epigenetic mechanism that regulates imprinted genes in the placenta is different from that which regulates the same genes in the embryo.
DNA methylation and repressive histone marks can be used to mark imprinted genes in different ways, and that the use of histone marks is not necessarily a less stable mechanism.
the IC2 region is not marked by parent specific DNA methyaltion, but rather by repressive histones marks.
